Chiricahua National Monument One Day Itinerary 

Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 11:12
Instaread

Get ready to have a full day of adventure with this one day itinerary for Chiricahua National Monument. Chiricahua is one of the less popular national park sites in Arizona. It’s known for its towering volcanic rock hoodoos and scenic mountain views. 

This park is located in a remote part of Arizona, making it less convenient to visit than many of the state’s more popular national parks. As a result, it is often overlooked and isn’t on many travelers’ Arizona bucket lists. It’s perfect if you’re looking for fewer crowds on the trail. Although it may not be as well known, there is no shortage of unique views here.

In this post I provide you with the perfect one day itinerary for Chiricahua so you can make the most of your day in the park.

Where is Chiricahua National Monument? 

Chiricahua National Monument is located in south eastern Arizona near the New Mexico border.


It really isn’t located near any major cities. The closest big town is Sierra Vista which is about 1.5 hours from Chiricahua. Tucson is the next closest city roughly 2.5 hours away.

Best Time to Visit Chiricahua

Spring (March-May) and Fall (September-November)

Spring and fall will provide you with the most comfortable temperatures for hiking. 

We actually visited Chiricahua in December and it was nice in the way that we had most of the trails to ourselves since it’s the off season. It was pretty cold though so if you visit in the winter you will want to bring some extra layers. Including a hat or gloves. 

Hiking can become dangerous during the summer in Arizona, so I wouldn’t recommend visiting between the months of June-August if your main goal is to spend your day hiking.

Chiricahua sits at a much higher elevation than cities like Phoenix and Tucson, which can help keep temperatures somewhat cooler during the summer. However, the dry desert heat can still be intense, especially if you’re not accustomed to it.

On the other hand, the higher elevation also means winters are much colder than many visitors expect. Be sure to check the forecast and pack accordingly, no matter what time of year you visit.

The Best Chiricahua One Day Itinerary

This National Monument covers a lot of land. You aren’t going to be able to do every single thing in one day. I wish we had more time in the park, but I think we squeezed in all the main things in Chiricahua in this one day itinerary.

Here’s what you won’t want to miss.

Look for Coatis at Faraway Ranch

As you begin your drive into the park I recommend, before going anywhere else, that you stop at the Faraway Ranch Trail. Faraway Ranch is one of the places in the park known to have coatimundis.

If you aren’t familiar, coatimundis (also known as just ‘coatis’) are raccoon-like mammals that are pretty rare to see in Arizona. Chiricahua National Monument is one of the few places that has frequent sightings of them.

However, you can only see them at the very beginning of the park. They cannot live up in the higher elevations.

We unfortunately didn’t see any on our visit, but a park ranger told us that Faraway Ranch is where he sees them roaming the most. So definitely walk this trail and try your luck at seeing a coati!

If you visit Faraway Ranch on your way in, then you won’t have to backtrack during your day and you can spend most of your time up where all the main hiking trails are.

Take the Bonita Canyon Scenic Drive Through Chiricahua

Once you’ve visited Faraway Ranch, you will want to continue your drive up through the park. 

The Bonita Canyon Dr is the main road in the park, and it is truly incredible to drive through. It’s an 8 mile paved road that ascends nearly 2,000 ft. of elevation.

The scenic drive starts at the bottom of the canyon before winding up through the forests of rock hoodoos. It ends at one of the highest points in the park (Massai Point) at 6,870 ft. 

Most of the best hikes at Chiricahua that you can incorporate into your one day itinerary are towards the end of the scenic drive. This is where all the trails through the hoodoos are that the park is known for.

There aren’t many overlooks or places to pull over and take in the views, but it’s just an amazing experience to watch the landscape change before your eyes as you drive.

Hike the Echo Canyon Grottos

The Echo Canyon Grottos Trail is probably the most popular hike in the park. It’s a 1 mile loop trail that takes you up close and personal inside caves or grottos formed by the hoodoos. 

I would rate this trail as easy due to having only about 80 ft. of elevation gain. It’s doable for most visitors.

However, the terrain is rocky. Some mild climbing over rocks is required at points. But overall if you’re a frequent hiker, you’ll have no problems here. 

The views you get from this hike are insane. Not only can you explore inside the grottos, but you will see the vast forest of hoodoos surrounding you. It’s really neat to hike right along them. This trail really puts it in perspective of how big these rocks are. 

The Echo Canyon Grottos is a must-see at Chiricahua. If you only want to do one hike, make it this one!

Hike to Inspiration Point

In your one day itinerary you should plan for at least one longer hike in Chiricahua to get the full experience hiking out in the more remote areas of the park. We decided to try out the Inspiration Point Trail. 

Inspiration Point is 5.5 miles with over 1,000 ft. elevation gain. The tough journey is worth it for what I consider to be the very best view in the park. 

We started this hike at the Massai Point Overlook, but you can also begin at the Echo Canyon Grottos if you want to make it one big hike. 

This hike is unique in the way that you begin a long gradual descent into the canyon just to climb back up the other side of it to get to the top where you’ll find Inspiration Point. 

The terrain is more difficult and rocky with mild rock scrambling required at times. So this is a more strenuous hike that will require snacks and plenty of water. Make sure you are prepared. 

At the end you’ll come out to a 360° overlook surrounded by the endless hoodoos. You’ll even be able to see the bottom of the canyon and Bonita Canyon Dr where you drove in at.

Alternative: Hike Heart of Rocks Loop

If we had more than one day in the park, I would’ve loved to try out the Heart of Rocks Loop. It’s supposedly another one of the best trails in Chiricahua and if it wasn’t so long we would’ve incorporated it into our one day itinerary too.

The Heart of Rocks Loop is about a 7 mile round trip with approximately 1,600 ft. of elevation gain. There are a few different places you can start for this hike (the Visitor Center, Maasai Point or Echo Canyon) but no matter where you start it will still be a long 7+ mile trek.

I can’t say much about it since we didn’t do it but I think it’s pretty comparable to Inspiration Point. 

If you’re feeling ambitious you can even do Echo Canyon Grottos, Inspiration Point, and Heart of Rocks all together since the trails all intertwine. Not sure the exact mileage for that but it would probably be at least 10 miles.

Watch the Sunset from Massai Point Overlook

The Massai Point Overlook can easily be reached via a short and paved 0.4 mile trail. If you aren’t quite up for hiking to Inspiration Point or the Heart of Rocks, this is a good alternative that will still give you amazing views with little effort. 

Like I said the Inspiration Point Trail begins from the Massai Point Overlook so when we ended our hike, we got back right in time for the sun to set. 

Since this is the highest point that you can drive to in the park you’ll get phenomenal views of the hoodoos around you during golden hour and as the sky begins to turn dark.

This is perfect for all visitors as it doesn’t require much hiking at all, but you still get a great elevated view of the setting sun.

Stargaze at Chiricahua National Monument

Chiricahua National Monument is one of Arizona’s International Dark Sky Places making it an amazing place to stargaze. 

This park is very remote. It’s surrounded by a lot of raw land and not near any big cities. If you get lucky with a clear night you will see so many beautiful stars. 

The park is always open and there is no entrance gate so you can come in at any time of the day. You can even come in at midnight just to stargaze.

If you plan on camping or staying in the area that night I definitely recommend you stay a few hours after the sunset to see the stars.

Is it Worth it to Spend One Day in Chiricahua?

Yes! There are a variety of different hikes suitable for all levels and the scenic drive through the park is spectacular. The hoodoo rock formations are such a unique thing to see since there’s nothing else really like it in Arizona.

The park is big enough to where it feels like there’s always new hikes to check out, yet small enough to where all you need is one day in the park to feel like you got the whole experience of Chiricahua. 

Other Things to Do Near Chiricahua

Despite being in a rural part of the state, there are a few great nearby attractions that are worth stopping at after your day at Chiricahua.

  • Coronado National Monument (1 hour 40 minutes from Chiricahua): Located on the Mexican border, Coronado is another NPS site preserving the history of the 1540 expedition led by Spanish explorer Francisco Vázquez de Coronado. You can take the scenic drive to Coronado Peak for sweeping views across Arizona and Mexico, or hike to Coronado Cave, a limestone cave that requires no technical gear.
  • Bisbee (1 hour 20 minutes from Chiricahua): One of Arizona’s most unique small towns. Once a thriving copper mining town, it’s now known for its colorful hillside homes, narrow winding streets, and vibrant arts scene.
  • Tombstone (1 hour 15 minutes from Chiricahua): The most iconic Wild West town in the US. Once a booming silver mining town in the 1880s, it’s now a popular destination for history buffs, cowboy enthusiasts, and travelers looking to step back in time.

I hope this guide gave you some inspiration on how to plan your one day itinerary in Chiricahua and thank you so much for reading!
